result.summary: Hymenaeus attends the wedding of Orpheus and Eurydice with ill omens, and Eurydice dies of a snake bite. Orpheus descends to the underworld and charms its rulers into releasing her on condition he not look back, but he does and loses her again. He mourns for years, shuns women and turns to boys.

scenes.title: Ill-omened wedding and Eurydice's death
scenes.summary: Hymenaeus comes to the wedding with a smoking torch and no good omens. Eurydice is bitten by a serpent while walking with the Naiads and dies.
scenes.stakes: Orpheus's marriage and his wife's life are destroyed by the omen-bearing wedding.

scenes.title: Orpheus pleads before the rulers
scenes.summary: Orpheus descends by the Tænarian gate and sings to Persephone and Pluto, asking them to restore Eurydice. Even the damned are stilled and the rulers yield.
scenes.stakes: Orpheus will refuse to return if denied, risking his own life as well as Eurydice's return.

scenes.title: Looking back
scenes.summary: Eurydice is released on condition Orpheus not look back. Near the upper earth he turns and she is lost a second time.
scenes.stakes: Orpheus risks losing Eurydice forever if he looks back before leaving the Avernian valleys.

scenes.title: Comparison to petrified figures
scenes.summary: Orpheus's shock is compared to that of the shepherd turned to stone by Cerberus, and Olenus and Lethaea turned to rock.

scenes.title: Grief and withdrawal
scenes.summary: The ferryman refuses Orpheus, who mourns seven days and retreats to Rhodope. He avoids women for three years and urges Thracians toward young men.
scenes.stakes: Orpheus is left in grief and isolation.

alias_notes.explanation: Named from Mount Rhodope in Thrace.

notable_quotes.reason: Orpheus's concise declaration that love overcame his resolve to endure.
Eurydice's gentle acceptance: why complain of being loved?

analysis.text: The passage shows love's power against death, and the loss caused by impatience and doubt. Art can move the underworld but cannot overcome fate's conditions.
Ovid's version emphasizes Orpheus's pathos and ends with the tradition of Thracian pederasty, framing the later songs in Book 10.

legacy.text: The tale inspired operas such as Monteverdi's L'Orfeo (1607) and Gluck's Orfeo ed Euridice (1762).
The musical Hadestown (2010 album, 2019 Broadway) retells Orpheus and Eurydice.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's account draws on Virgil's Georgics Book 4, which popularized the looking-back detail.

language_notes.text: Hymenæus is the god of weddings, invoked in marriage songs. His failure to bless this wedding signals disaster.
Rhodopeïan: from Mount Rhodope in Thrace, Orpheus's homeland. The Tænarian gate was a cave in southern Greece believed to lead to the underworld.
"Ruler of the shades" is Pluto, the god of the dead; Persephone is his queen.
The "threefold throat" belongs to Cerberus, the dog guarding the underworld. Orpheus says he has not come to chain him, as Hercules did.
"The rape of former days": Pluto's abduction of Proserpina (Persephone), which Orpheus suggests was driven by love.
"Weave over again the thread" refers to the Fates spinning and cutting each life's thread. He asks them to restore Eurydice's life.
These are famous damned figures: Tantalus (thirst), Ixion (wheel), Tityus (liver), the Belides (water jars), Sisyphus (stone). Orpheus's song suspends their punishments.
Eumenides: the Furies, avenging goddesses who punish crimes. Their weeping is unprecedented.
The Rhodopeïan hero is Orpheus, a Thracian, since Mount Rhodope is in Thrace. 'Avernian vallies' means the valleys of the underworld, named for Lake Avernus, a reputed entrance.
Ovid compares Orpheus to figures turned to stone: a man who saw Cerberus, Olenus and Lethaea. Their stories are only hinted at, so the reader must know or infer them.
'Gifts of Ceres' means bread or grain; Ceres was goddess of agriculture. Orpheus fasts for seven days.
The 'third Titan' is the sun, and the 'year bounded by the Fishes' means the sun passed through all the zodiac signs ending at Pisces. Three years have passed.
'On this side of manhood' means before boys reach full manhood. Orpheus urges love of youths in their brief springtime.

context_notes.text: A wedding torch was part of the ceremony. A smoking, flameless torch was a bad omen.
Naiads are nymphs of springs and streams, here companions of the bride.
The ferryman is Charon, who rowed the dead across the river of the underworld. Orpheus had charmed him on the way down, but now he is refused.
Rhodope and Hæmus are mountain ranges in Thrace, Orpheus's homeland, where he retreats to mourn.

literary_notes.text: The weeping smoke and dead flame foretell the bride's death and the marriage's failure.
Love is treated as a powerful being who overcomes Orpheus's efforts at endurance.
Orpheus's bitter invitation to "triumph" in both deaths turns the rulers' victory into a plea for pity.
The whole catalogue of suspended torments shows the overwhelming power of Orpheus's song. It is enumeration, not literal count.
Briefly the narrator turns to address Sisyphus directly in the previous sentence, heightening the scene's emotion.
The narrator's exclamation 'hapless one!' expresses pity for Eurydice and directs the reader's sympathy to her.
Eurydice's question shows her acceptance and love; she does not blame him, which makes the loss more pathetic.
Orpheus's stunned grief is compared to people turned to stone, suggesting he is frozen by loss. A chain of examples extends the comparison.
Grief and tears are called his 'sustenance', as though sorrow replaced food, showing the depth of his mourning.
